items.prompt: What is trade-off pushback, as defined in this unit?
choices: Refusing a request outright to protect your own time and workload
Naming the real constraint behind a request and offering concrete options, then letting the requester decide
Agreeing to every incoming request without question, just to avoid conflict
Escalating every ambiguous request straight to a manager instead of answering it
items.explanation: Trade-off pushback is neither refusal nor silent acceptance — it surfaces the actual constraint and concrete options, then hands the decision back to the person who owns the priority.
items.reference:
Trade-off pushback
name the real constraint
offer concrete options
hand the decision back

Why: Neither refusing nor silently accepting — surfacing the real trade-off instead.

items.prompt: Which response is an example of trade-off pushback?
choices: 'No, I'm too busy to take this on right now.'
'Sure, I'll figure it out somehow, don't worry about it.'
'I can do this, but it means the migration slips a week — is that okay?'
'Let me think about it and get back to you — never, as it turns out.'
items.explanation: This response names a specific trade-off (the migration slipping) and asks the requester to decide — the defining shape of trade-off pushback.
items.reference:
Trade-off pushback
name the real constraint
offer concrete options
hand the decision back

Why: Neither refusing nor silently accepting — surfacing the real trade-off instead.

items.prompt: Why can a flat 'no' damage trust even when it's the technically correct call?
choices: Because a flat 'no' is always the objectively wrong answer to give
Because it doesn't reveal the actual reasoning, so the requester can't tell if it's a real constraint or just reluctance
Because saying a flat 'no' takes too long to actually say out loud
Because requests of any kind should never be declined under any circumstances
items.explanation: Without the actual constraint visible, a flat 'no' can't be evaluated or negotiated by the requester — it just reads as a closed door.
items.reference:
Why a flat 'no' backfires
hides the reasoning
requester can't evaluate or negotiate

Why: A conclusion without its reasoning reads as a closed door rather than a fact to work with.

items.prompt: A colleague says 'no' to a request without explanation, more than once. What's the likely long-term effect?
choices: The requester will always assume there's a good, legitimate reason behind it
The requester starts reading them as uncooperative, whether or not the constraint was real
There's no lasting effect on the relationship between them over time at all
The requester will stop making any requests of them at all, which is ideal
items.explanation: Repeated unexplained refusals erode trust regardless of whether each individual 'no' was actually justified — the requester has no way to distinguish a real constraint from reluctance.
items.reference:
Why a flat 'no' backfires
hides the reasoning
requester can't evaluate or negotiate

Why: A conclusion without its reasoning reads as a closed door rather than a fact to work with.

items.prompt: Why is a silent 'yes' to an overloaded request actually worse for the relationship than it feels in the moment?
choices: It isn't actually worse at all — it's always the objectively safer choice to make
The cost doesn't disappear, it just shows up later as a missed commitment the requester never agreed to
Silent agreement always leads to better results than openly naming a trade-off
It only really matters when the work in question is technical in nature
items.explanation: The trade-off still happens — it's just discovered later, unplanned, which reads as a broken commitment rather than a trade the requester consciously accepted.
items.reference:
Why silent 'yes' backfires
cost doesn't disappear
it lands later, unplanned, unagreed

Why: A smooth moment now can become a broken commitment later, once the hidden cost surfaces.

As a broken commitment, since they were never told a trade-off was happening

As proof that the person doing the work is highly capable and reliable
items.explanation: Because the trade-off was never surfaced, the requester experiences the slipped commitment as broken trust rather than an informed decision they made.
items.reference:
Why silent 'yes' backfires
cost doesn't disappear
it lands later, unplanned, unagreed

Why: A smooth moment now can become a broken commitment later, once the hidden cost surfaces.

items.prompt: What makes a stated constraint 'concrete' rather than vague, per this unit?
choices: It's stated loudly, firmly, and with visible confidence behind it
It's a checkable fact ('committed to X and Y') rather than a feeling ('I'm too busy')
It's delivered in writing rather than said out loud in conversation
It includes a sincere apology for not being able to help sooner
items.explanation: A concrete constraint is something the requester can actually verify or reason about — a specific commitment, not a vague feeling of business.
items.reference:
A concrete constraint
not: 'I'm too busy' (a feeling)
yes: 'sprint is committed to X and Y' (checkable)

Why: The requester needs something they can actually evaluate, not just a feeling.

A concrete constraint

let the priority owner decide how to spend it
